lessons.title: Contract Specifications — Lot Size, Tick Size, Expiry, and Settlement

children.text: Every year, a few first-time commodity traders discover the hard way that a gold futures position does not simply vanish if you forget about it. They hold a Gold Mini contract a little too close to expiry, miss the notices from their broker, and wake up to find they are on the hook to either accept delivery of physical gold at an exchange-approved vault or scramble to close the position at whatever price is available. None of this is a glitch. It is exactly what the contract specification said would happen, and almost nobody reads the contract specification.

body.text: A contract specification is the exchange's rulebook for one futures contract: how much of the commodity one lot represents, the smallest price move that counts, when the contract stops trading, and how it finally settles. Every number in this lesson comes from that rulebook, not from you or your broker.

children.text: Lot Size: How Much You're Actually Trading

markDefs.definition: The fixed quantity of the underlying commodity that one futures contract represents. You cannot buy half a lot or 1.5 lots; positions move in whole-lot increments.

children.text: The
lot size

is fixed by the exchange and cannot be negotiated. Notice below how MCX offers several sizes of the same underlying, gold, precisely so that a small trader and a bullion dealer can both participate at a lot size that fits their capital.

body.caption: Illustrative lot sizes: same commodity, different scale (always confirm current specifications on the exchange website, as they can change)

stats.label: 1 lot Gold Mini
stats.context: 100 g at an illustrative ₹60,000 per 10 g

stats.label: 1 lot Crude Oil
stats.context: 100 barrels at an illustrative ₹6,000 per barrel

stats.label: 1 lot Silver
stats.context: 30 kg at an illustrative ₹90,000 per kg

stats.label: 1 lot Chana
stats.context: 100 quintals (10 tonnes) at an illustrative ₹6,500 per quintal

body.text: Contract value equals lot size multiplied by price. This is the number that determines your real market exposure, not the margin you put up to trade it. Chapter 2's next lesson shows exactly how margin relates to this contract value.

children.text: Tick Size: The Smallest Price Move That Counts

markDefs.definition: The minimum amount by which a contract's quoted price is allowed to move. Prices cannot tick in fractions smaller than this.

children.text: The
tick size

is set on the quoted unit, not on the lot, which is exactly why it is easy to get the tick value wrong. MCX gold contracts, across the Gold, Gold Mini, Guinea and Petal variants, all move in steps of ₹1 per 10 grams. But since each variant has a different lot size, the same tick is worth a different amount of money depending on which contract you are trading.

body.caption: The rupee value of the smallest possible price move, for one lot.

body.title: Same tick size, different contract
body.prompt: MCX Gold moves in ticks of ₹1 per 10 grams, and one lot of Gold is 1 kg (100 units of 10 grams). What is the rupee value of one tick for one lot of Gold?
body.explanation: 1 kg is 100 times 10 grams, so one tick of ₹1 per 10 grams moves the full lot by ₹1 × 100 = ₹100.

body.title: Now do it for Gold Mini
body.prompt: Gold Mini has the same ₹1 per 10 gram tick size, but its lot size is only 100 grams (10 units of 10 grams). What is the rupee value of one tick for one lot of Gold Mini?
body.explanation: 100 grams is 10 times 10 grams, so one tick is worth ₹1 × 10 = ₹10 for a Gold Mini lot, one-tenth of the ₹100 tick value on the full-size Gold contract, purely because the lot size is smaller.

children.text: Expiry: Contracts Don't Live Forever

markDefs.definition: The calendar month in which a specific futures contract stops trading and settles. An exchange typically lists several contract months for the same commodity at once, so you choose which month's contract to trade.

children.text: Unlike a share, a futures contract has a built-in expiry date, after which it ceases to exist. Exchanges list multiple
contract months

for the same underlying at once. MCX gold, for instance, typically has up to six contract months trading simultaneously, expiring on or around the 5th of the contract month, while MCX crude oil, being far more sensitive to fast-moving global news, is listed with shorter monthly contracts expiring around the 19th or 20th. The nearest contract, called the near-month or front-month contract, is usually the most heavily traded and has the tightest bid-ask spreads. As it nears expiry, traders wanting to keep their exposure alive without settling must
roll over
: close the expiring contract and open an equivalent position in the next contract month.

body.title: Near-month vs far-month
body.question: You want to place a large order and care most about getting filled close to the current market price, with minimal slippage. Which contract month should you generally prefer, all else equal?
options: The far-month contract, since it gives you more time before expiry
The near-month (front-month) contract, since it is usually the most liquid with the tightest spreads
It does not matter which month you choose
Whichever month has the highest price
body.explanation: Liquidity is usually concentrated in the near-month contract. Far-month contracts can have wide bid-ask spreads and thin order books, which increases slippage on large orders.

children.text: Settlement: Cash vs Physical Delivery

markDefs.definition: A settlement method where the contract closes by paying or receiving the price difference in rupees, with no physical commodity changing hands.
A settlement method where a trader still holding a position at expiry must actually give or take delivery of the physical commodity at an exchange-accredited warehouse or vault.

children.text: This is where contracts split into two very different endings. MCX crude oil is
cash-settled

: on expiry, its final settlement price is derived from NYMEX WTI crude's own settlement price, converted to rupees using the RBI's reference exchange rate, and every open position is simply squared off in cash at that price. Nobody in India ends up owning barrels of crude oil. MCX Gold and Gold Mini, by contrast, are
compulsory delivery

contracts. If you are still holding a position when the delivery process, known as the tender period, opens in the final days before expiry, you are obligated to give or take delivery of physical gold that meets the exchange's purity standard, stored at a WDRA-accredited vault.

body.title: Cash settlement vs compulsory physical delivery

columns.label: Cash settlement (e.g. MCX Crude Oil)
points: Settles as a cash difference against a reference price at expiry
No warehouse, no vault, no logistics
Suits commodities that are impractical or costly to physically deliver domestically
The whole position, hedger or speculator, is closed out automatically

columns.label: Compulsory delivery (e.g. MCX Gold, Gold Mini)
points: A position held into the tender period must give or take physical delivery
Requires an accredited vault or warehouse and quality certification
Suits durable, storable commodities where genuine buyers and sellers want the option to actually trade the physical good
Retail speculators are expected to square off or roll over well before the tender period begins

body.text: If you have no intention of ever giving or taking physical delivery, mark your calendar for a few trading days before a compulsory-delivery contract's tender period opens, not the expiry date itself. By the time the tender period begins, it is often too late to simply change your mind.

body.title: The forgotten Gold Mini position
body.scenario: Deepa bought 1 lot of MCX Gold Mini three months ago as a short-term trade and simply forgot about it, since the price barely moved and she stopped checking it. Her broker's app now shows a notice that the contract's tender period begins in two trading sessions.
body.prompt: What are Deepa's realistic options at this point, and what would have avoided this situation entirely?
body.modelAnswer: Deepa can either square off her position in the market before the tender period begins, converting her futures exposure into a cash profit or loss, or roll it over into a later contract month if she wants to keep the exposure alive without taking delivery. If she does neither and the tender period opens while she still holds the position, she may be required to actually take delivery of 100 grams of physical gold at an accredited vault, along with the associated delivery logistics and costs. The simplest fix is to never treat a compulsory-delivery contract as a 'set and forget' position, and to track the contract's specific expiry and tender period dates from the start.

cards.definition: The fixed quantity of the underlying commodity one futures contract represents.
The minimum permitted price movement of a contract, set on the quoted unit.
The rupee value of one tick move for a full lot; tick size multiplied by lot size (adjusted for the quotation unit).
The calendar month in which a specific futures contract expires and settles.
Closing a position in an expiring contract and opening an equivalent position in a later contract month, to keep exposure alive without settling.
Settling a contract by paying or receiving a price difference in cash, with no physical commodity delivered.
A settlement method requiring a position held into the tender period to give or take actual physical delivery of the commodity.
The window shortly before expiry during which a compulsory-delivery contract's actual physical delivery process takes place.

points: Lot size, fixed by the exchange, determines how much of a commodity one contract represents; contract value equals lot size times price.
Tick size is set on the quoted unit, so the same tick size can be worth very different amounts across contract variants with different lot sizes.
Every futures contract has an expiry, and exchanges list several contract months at once. Liquidity usually concentrates in the near-month contract, and traders roll over to keep exposure alive.

Settlement is either cash (like MCX crude oil, settled against a converted NYMEX WTI price) or compulsory physical delivery (like MCX Gold and Gold Mini, settled at an accredited vault during the tender period).
If you never intend to take or give delivery, track the tender period date, not just the expiry date, and square off or roll over well ahead of it.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Lot sizes, tick sizes, expiry conventions and settlement methods are set by the exchange and change from time to time; always verify the current contract specification on the MCX or NCDEX website before trading.
